content.content:
The marker stack is one file at one path, and it belongs to one working copy. Where the file is has already been fixed: `.deccy/markers.json`, in the deccy state directory under the store root (ysqqrqsp). Nothing here relocates that file, renames it, or makes a copy of it, and nothing here adds a second one — the fixed path is the whole of the answer to where the stack is. What is left to this decision is the other half of the same sentence: which working copy reads that file and which working copy writes it. The answer is the trunk workspace, and no other. A draft workspace never reads the marker stack and never writes it: the one file at the fixed path is not in a draft's tree, no second marker file is created there or beside the draft, and no per-draft stack is kept anywhere.

The trunk workspace is a working copy, and it is named by place. It is the working copy from which a landing is invoked, and whose store root is the one that holds `.deccy/markers.json`; both clauses pick out the same working copy, because the state directory is a directory of the repository's own working copy (xqzstoyo), so the working copy whose root contains the store root is that one, while a landing reaches its draft by the record's handle and reads the draft's content where the draft carries it (uvrltuvo), so the draft never has to be the working copy the invocation runs in. Nothing else is part of the definition. No change id makes a working copy the trunk, no workspace name does, and neither "the main workspace" nor any other label is one of the terms: the trunk is the working copy that holds the store root, and it is the trunk after it is renamed and after it is checked out at a different change, because what is named is a place where the state directory lives and not a label and not a change.

A draft workspace is never the trunk. A draft's workspace lies under one per-user root outside the repository, at the directory derived from the record's handle (xqzstoyo), and it is another working copy of the repository's tree, not another place where the state directory sits. Its root therefore never contains the state directory, `.deccy/markers.json` under it would be a different file at a different path, and to read or write that file there would be to make a second marker file and a stack per draft — exactly what the fixed place forecloses (ysqqrqsp). A draft needs no stack of its own to be opened, edited, reviewed or landed: the stack is read and written only by the invocations that bracket (vwlrqoxk), and those run in the trunk.

A landing brackets in the trunk, once. Every operation runs bracketed (pmxnnvvq), and only creation, recording and removal invocations bracket (vwlrqoxk). A landing is a recording — `deccy record --from <handle> --to <node>` is the recording `deccy record <path>... --to <id>` already is, reached through a different selection of the edits, creating no node and no change (uvrltuvo) — so a landing is one of the invocations that bracket and it draws exactly one bracket, over its own run window. That bracket is drawn on the trunk's marker file: the opening and closing markers are written in the working copy that holds the store root, by the invocation the caller ran, for the one operation it performed. There is no second bracket for the landing, no bracket on any registry write, and no fourth invocation brought into the bracketing set (vwlrqoxk). The `landed` write that marks the draft's record is partial work inside the recording and is not bracketed apart (qvkuluyw), and the recording it rides in is the landing and not a second landing or a second verb beside it (uvrltuvo). The record document a draft's opening writes is a registry write — it creates no node and no change, records no edit into a node and removes nothing (qvkuluyw) — so it is not an operation and is never bracketed either.

Draft-side work is not bracketed, and a landing's reads are not draft-side work. Work performed in the draft workspace — opening the draft, and the drafter's own jj edits in that working copy — is not bracketed and touches no marker, because it is not one of the three bracketing invocations (vwlrqoxk) and the draft's edits enter a node's change only when the landing records them (uvrltuvo). This does not say that a landing may not read the draft's working copy. A landing reads the changed owned paths the draft carries, comparing the content the draft holds for a path with the content the target change holds for it (uvrltuvo), and those reads happen while the landing runs, so they lie inside the landing's one bracket and within the run window that bracket draws (pmxnnvvq). A read taken in the draft's directory by a trunk-side landing is part of the recording; it is not work performed in the draft workspace, it does not bracket, and it does not move the stack, which stays the file in the trunk the same invocation is writing its markers to.

These clauses are one commitment. The file's place is fixed (ysqqrqsp); which working copy can hold it follows from where a state directory sits and where a draft's workspace sits (xqzstoyo), and only the trunk can hold the store root; and how many brackets a landing draws follows from what a landing is (uvrltuvo) and from what brackets (pmxnnvvq, vwlrqoxk, qvkuluyw). Take away the trunk's ownership and the stack would have to be duplicated per workspace, contradicting the fixed path; take away the single bracket and the landing would either bracket twice, leaving undo a unit beside the recording, or bracket its registry write, bringing the registry into the operation vocabulary through the door qvkuluyw closes. The answers hold together or not at all: one file, in the trunk, one bracket, on the recording.

Not settled here. The cap on open records and the barrier over them, the surface that lists drafts, how a handle is minted or a draft opened, the wording, stream, exit status and testing order of any refusal, the encoding of the content comparison a landing takes, and the marker format and marker content are none of them decided here (uvrltuvo, qvkuluyw). Nor is a particular change named as the trunk: the marker stack is held by a working copy, the file's place is fixed relative to that working copy's store root and not relative to a change, and the change a given invocation happens to have checked out is not part of what this ownership says.

The decision's own summary: the marker stack belongs to the trunk workspace, defined by place; draft workspaces neither read nor write it; and a landing brackets in the trunk while draft-side work is not bracketed.
content.rationale:
The marker file's place was already settled and this node does not touch it: `.deccy/markers.json`, in the state directory under the store root (ysqqrqsp). What that leaves unstated is which working copy of a repository performs the read and the write, and without an answer the path alone cannot tell a bracket in the trunk from a bracket in a draft. Placing the stack by working copy answers exactly that and nothing more: it does not move the file, rename it, or give any workspace a second one.

The working copy is chosen by place rather than by identity. The state directory is a directory of the repository's own working copy (xqzstoyo), so the working copy whose root contains the store root is that one; a draft workspace is a working copy of the same tree placed under a per-user root outside the repository at the directory its handle names (xqzstoyo), so its root is not the store root and a marker file under it would be a different file at a different path. Naming the trunk by change id or by workspace name would be a definition that has to be rewritten when a working copy is renamed or checks out something else; naming it by the place that holds the store root survives both, and it is the only property that makes the fixed path resolve to one file.

The bracket count follows from the prerequisites rather than being chosen. A landing is a recording (uvrltuvo), every operation is bracketed (pmxnnvvq), and only creation, recording and removal invocations bracket (vwlrqoxk); so the landing draws one bracket and it is the bracket of that recording. The tempting additions are all closed: a second bracket for the landing would split one operation into two undoable units, a bracket on the `landed` write would make the registry's update an operation of its own (qvkuluyw), a bracket on the opening of a draft would be a fourth bracketing invocation (vwlrqoxk), and putting the bracket on some other verb would re-create the landing uvrltuvo says does not exist. Saying the landing brackets in the trunk is therefore not a new rule beside those four; it is the place where the one bracket they already require is written.

The draft side is the part most easily misread, so it is said twice and in both directions. Work performed in the draft workspace — opening the draft, the drafter's own jj edits — is never bracketed: it is not one of the three bracketing invocations (vwlrqoxk), the draft's edits are not in a node's change until a landing records them (uvrltuvo), and the record the opening writes is a registry write, which is not an operation at all (qvkuluyw). But a landing invoked at the trunk reads the draft's working copy, because the changed owned paths are exactly the content the draft carries for the node's owned set (uvrltuvo); those reads are inside the landing's run window and inside its one bracket (pmxnnvvq). Reading the draft is not work in the draft, and it neither brackets nor needs a stack in the draft's directory. This is the distinction that keeps the node from being read as a claim that the trunk never touches a draft's workspace.

What is left out is left out because a prerequisite defers it: the cap and the barrier, the drafts listing surface, handle minting and the opening verb, refusal wording and exit status, and the content-identity encoding all belong to other commitments (uvrltuvo, qvkuluyw). The trunk is also not named as a change: a working copy is what holds a state directory, the file's path is fixed relative to the store root, and which change the working copy has checked out is not part of the ownership this node settles.
